items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: “that’s Charlie Shavers—that’s Dizzy—that’s Louis Armstrong—that’s Red Allen.”

ctx.x: Well I’ve, in my era, there was so much competition. It was very competitive in New York at that time. And Charlie Shavers, and so many good trumpet players and they all

had their own style. They had their own sound. There was no doubt when you heard them playing you could be ten miles away and hear them play and say, “that’s Charlie Shavers—that’s Dizzy—that’s Louis Armstrong—that’s Red Allen.” Bunny Berigan had a good sound of his own. But Teddy Wilson, he had a style which was simple but beautiful, you know?
And the Basie band itself had a style.

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Fats Navarro, Freddy Webster, Red Allen, Rex Stuart, there was just so many great guys you could learn from.

ctx.x: Do you remember some of the other groups you heard, bands you heard right on that first couple of days when you arrived?

Art Tatum…I walked up 7th Avenue and there was Ellington walking up the street and the next thing you know Claude Hopkins is walking up the street. Louis Armstrong, I’d see him on 7th Avenue. They’d all walk up and down 7th Avenue. Oh man, I said, gee, can you top this? I’m standing there just looking at them because most of the times I had seen them was on the stage and I’m out in the audience and here I am just about ready to shake his hand. Oh my goodness. After you get through work, you go up to Monroe’s…
Were you sitting in much or just listening?

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Oh, he was one of my idols. Oh, yeah, Red Allen was one of my idols because he played in the part of the horn, the register on the horn, that I loved to play in, you see.

ctx.x: I mean, there's a little bit of Red Allen, I would think.

Oh, he was one of my idols. Oh, yeah, Red Allen was one of my idols because he played in the part of the horn, the register on the horn, that I loved to play in, you see. And then, I think he was sort of the same -- he felt the same way I did, because there's only going to be one Louie Armstrong. And in the first place, I didn't have the chops to play like Louie Armstrong. I didn't have the chops to play like Roy. They are phenomenons, you know. So the lines I played --
